newsitem.title: FRANCE: No Algerian solution possible from outside--France.
newsitem.headline: No Algerian solution possible from outside--France.

text.p: Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, stressing French efforts to steer clear of Algeria's civil war, said on Tuesday a solution to the conflict could not come from outside.
"The solution must come from inside. I do not believe a solution can come from outside...and everyone knows a solution to the crisis must be political," de Charette told parliament.
"It is up to Algeria and to the Algerians to decide (on their future). As far as France is concerned, we will always be on the side of democracy," he said.

De Charette had to telephone his Algerian colleague Ahmed Attaf at the weekend to try to defuse a row over whether Paris was meddling in the North African country where civil strife has claimed 60,000 lives in five years.
He told Attaf France's official policy of non-interference in Algeria had not changed, officials said.
The row began when former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called last week for Islamists to be allowed to take part in forthcoming Algerian general elections.
Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin urged France to consult its European partners on a joint initiative on Algeria.
Jospin said no one dared to discuss the conflict while Paris stayed silent about Algeria, which won independence from France in 1962 after a bloody war.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Monday that Algeria's proposed parliamentary elections should be open to all legal parties, effectively ruling out the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).
He voiced horror at worsening violence in Algeria, a former French colony, and compassion for its population, adding that France had no desire to interfere in Algerian affairs.
Violence flared in Algeria after military-backed authorities cancelled a general election in January 1992 which the FIS was poised to win.
Paris is especially attuned to events across the Mediterranean because of the presence in France of more than two million people of Algerian origin.

Algerian-based Islamic fundamentalist groups claimed responsibilty for several bloody bombings in France in 1995 and authorities suspect them of a similar attack in Paris in December which killed four people.
The bombers were backed by several support groups recruited among Moslems in France of which about 200 people are currently in jail awaiting trial.
